name: Caramel
lede: Caramel is a warm golden brown named for toasted sugar, and the same word also names a food coloring.

sections.title: Toasted sugar
sections.body:
Paterson defines caramel as a pale brown, the color of toasted sugar [1]. The same dictionary has a separate entry for burnt sugar caramel as a deep yellowy brown [1]. So the word covers a range, from pale to deep, and the swatch here is a deep golden brown near [[toffee]], [[butterscotch]] and [[cinnamon]].

Caramel is also a food coloring, E150, and Paterson notes that one US company makes 62 types of caramel color for convenience foods [1].

sections.title: Seen in other words
sections.body: Finlay describes the walls of the Chauvet cave as having a swirling caramel effect from natural yellow stain [2]. She also reports natural-colored cotton in shades like caramel or café au lait, which grew stronger with washing [3]. Pastoureau lists chocolate caramel creams among the dishes of an all-black banquet menu he describes [4]. In each case the word is a description, not a pigment name; for a pigment-based neighbor see [[coffee]].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds the color in 553 of 23,781 paintings, 2.33 percent, as photographed [5]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 29 of 945 paintings, about 1.9 times the baseline [5]. Inside a painting it is mostly an accent, in 74 percent of 350 paintings [5]. The most devoted painter is George Dawe, in 13 of 50 works here [5]. It shares canvases with Warm Brown and Harvest Gold [5]. Aged varnish yellows paint, which pushes many browns toward caramel [5].

origin.source: Paterson, A Dictionary of Colour, "caramel" and "burnt sugar caramel"
